SEO and visibility
What is SEO? A plain starter guide for small shops

Right now, your next customer is searching Google for something you sell. SEO is how your shop turns up among the answers. It is not magic, and it is not a promise of ranking first. It is a set of concrete jobs, and you can start them this week.
25 November 2026·8 min read·The dadmor team

In this article

  1. What is SEO, in shop language?
  2. What SEO is not: three claims that should scare you off
  3. Step zero: a site of your own that Google can find
  4. Step one: the words customers actually search
  5. Step two: a product page that answers real questions
  6. Step three: trust and freshness
  7. How do you know it is working?
  8. The bottom line

Summary

  1. SEO means your site gets found for the searches real customers make, and gives them the right answer when they arrive. It starts with the site itself, not with tricks and shortcuts.
  2. Nobody can guarantee first place on Google. Keep your distance from anyone who promises it. Read your SEO results in Google Search Console, not in a seller’s promise.
  3. The right order for a small shop: a findable site of your own, product pages with correct titles and complete content, trust signals, and fresh content. That is enough to start.

Think about the last time you wanted to buy something and did not know the seller. What did you do? You probably searched Google. Your customers do the same. Even the ones who follow your page usually search the product name on Google once before buying, to compare prices and places.

SEO is short for search engine optimization. Do not let the name fool you. In practice it means building and writing your site so that when someone looks for your product, Google shows your site too, and the customer finds exactly what they came for.
This guide is written for small shops. No big agency budget, no heavy jargon. We go through the first steps in order, and we say plainly, right from the start, what SEO is not.
What is SEO, in shop language?

Picture Google as the busiest street in the city. Thousands of people walk it every day looking for a shop like yours. Google does the signposting: from each shop’s name and description, it decides which ones to show each customer.

SEO work means making your shop’s sign clear, that is, correct titles and descriptions. Keeping the inside of the shop tidy, that is, complete and fast pages. And having people speak well of your shop, that is, real trust and a real track record. That is exactly what Google is looking for: the best answer for the right person. Everything in this article comes back to one of these three.
What SEO is not: three claims that should scare you off

items: It is not a promise of ranking first: nobody can guarantee the first rank on Google. Rank depends on the search itself, the city, the competitors and time, and it sits in Google’s hands. Anyone selling a “guaranteed first rank” either does not know that, or knows it and says it anyway.

It is not tricks and shortcuts: bought links and pages stuffed with repeated keywords may work for a while. Then Google finds them, and the penalty is dropping from the very place you worked to reach.

It is not overnight work: getting seen on Google comes from weeks and months of staying put and doing things properly. SEO is like renting a shop on the busy street, not buying a billboard for one night.

blocks.html: We tell our own customers exactly this, and it is written on this site too: zero ranking promises, zero guaranteed results. If someone tells you the opposite, spend your money elsewhere.
Step zero: a site of your own that Google can find

SEO only means something on a site that is yours, and that Google can find. An Instagram page barely exists in Google search, and on a shop builder your control is limited. We open both up fully in Instagram page or website and Shop builder or your own website. On your own site, check these basics:

items: Your site opens correctly, and quickly, on mobile. Most of your customers arrive on a phone.
Every page has its own clear address, so Google can find each one.
Your site is registered in Google Search Console, Google’s own free tool, which shows you whether your site is being seen at all.

blocks.html: Step one: the words customers actually search

Customers do not talk like you. You know your product’s exact technical name. Your customer searches what is in their head: the simple product name, what it is for, sometimes their city. Simple ways to find those words:

items: Watch Google’s own suggestions as you start typing. Those are real searches, by real people.
Ask your customers: “What did you search to find us?” Write the answers down. That list is worth more to you than any tool.
Write each product page title in that same language: the product name plus the feature the customer is after. Not your warehouse code, not your internal name.

blocks.html: And one simple rule: one page, one topic. One page for one search. Cramming every product onto a single page confuses your customer and Google alike.
Step two: a product page that answers real questions
Google lifts the page that answers the customer’s question best. A complete product page has these:

items: A real, clear photo of the product itself. Not a catalogue photo lifted from someone else’s site.
A visible price and stock state; customers have no patience for asking prices in DMs, and for Google too, a page without a price is an unfinished page.
Text that answers the questions: what it is made of, its size, who and what it is for, how it ships, and how it can be returned.
A correct title and short description, because that is the exact thing your customer sees on Google, and clicks because of.

blocks.html: A page that answers the customer’s questions gets seen better on Google, and sells more when the customer arrives. The two are not separate jobs. We cover the second half fully in Traffic but no sales.
Google is looking for the best answer for the customer, not the best trick. A page that genuinely helps the customer finds its place, sooner or later.
Step three: trust and freshness

items: Put the trust symbol and real contact details on the site. We walk through the steps in Payment gateway and trust symbol. Google and customers both trust a shop with no address less.
Show real customer reviews on the product page, with names and dates. A real review and a made up one can be told apart from a distance.
Keep the site alive: new products, current prices, fresh content now and then. A site nobody has touched for a year looks, to Google too, like a shop with its shutters down.

blocks.html: How do you know it is working?

Google Search Console is free, and it shows you three things: which searches people find you with, how many people saw your site on Google and how many clicked, and which pages have problems. Look at it once a month. Read your SEO growth there: more searches and more pages, over several months. Any other report, especially a promise of an exact rank, is words, not evidence.

If you have neither the time nor the patience for this work, you can hand it to someone. Judge them by the same measures: concrete work and Search Console reports, not ranking promises. On our marketing content page we explain how we write content for shops, and how we report it.
The bottom line

For a small shop, SEO starts here: a site of your own, product pages written in your customer’s language that answer their questions, trust signals, and Search Console to check you are going the right way. Nobody can promise you a rank. But being found can be built, step by step, with patience.
Where do you start?

If you do not have a site yet, your SEO starts with building the site itself, and the project estimator shows its cost plainly. If you have a site and want its content written so customers and Google can both find it, see the marketing content page.
Frequently asked questions

How long does SEO take to show results?

For a small shop, being seriously seen on Google usually takes months, not days, and it depends on the competition for your product and your city. Anyone who promises an exact time and an exact rank is selling something that is not theirs to sell.

Can I do my own site’s SEO?

The steps in this article, yes: correct page titles and descriptions, complete product content, registering your site in Search Console, and keeping the site alive. The more technical work, and a steady content program, are what many shops later hand to a person or a team.

Which matters more, SEO or Instagram ads?

They do different jobs. Ads bring people quickly, and end quickly. SEO builds more slowly, but it stays, and it is yours. Most shops start with ads and build SEO alongside, so their dependence on ads shrinks over time.

Someone offers a guaranteed first rank on Google for a monthly fee. Should I accept?

No. Nobody can guarantee the first rank, because it is in Google’s hands and depends on the search and the competitors. From anyone you hire for SEO, ask for concrete work and Search Console reports. Not ranking promises.
